name: Leptin

lead: Leptin is a hormone made mostly by fat cells. Its levels track body fat, and the brain, mainly the hypothalamus, uses the signal to regulate hunger and energy use. It was reported by Jeffrey Friedman's lab in 1994.

For appearance it matters because dieting lowers leptin, which is thought to raise hunger, and because sleep and eating patterns also shift it. Fat-loss and cutting communities discuss leptin when explaining plateaus and appetite changes.

paras: People do not usually take leptin. They discuss ways of managing it indirectly: sleep, diet breaks, refeeds, exercise and eating schedules, all of which studies have linked to leptin levels.
Leptin itself is not a consumer product. Metreleptin, a synthetic analog, is prescribed for leptin deficiency and lipodystrophy. Many people with obesity have high leptin but reduced response to it.

chain: Leptin rises and falls with fat stores
Dieting and short sleep lower it
Affects how easily someone stays lean
angle.text: Leptin is a regulator of appetite rather than a treatment. People in fat-loss communities refer to it when planning diets, sleep and refeeds around staying lean.

lead: Leptin is a protein hormone made mostly by fat cells. The name comes from the Greek word for thin, and it was the first fat-derived hormone (adipokine) identified, in 1994 by Jeffrey Friedman's laboratory [1][2]. Blood levels rise with body fat and fall with fasting, so the brain, mainly the hypothalamus, uses leptin as a running report of stored energy when it adjusts hunger and energy use [1].

Leptin matters for appearance through body composition. People who diet down for leanness meet its effects as hunger, cravings and stalled fat loss, and fat-loss and cutting communities discuss it to explain why the last stretch of a diet feels harder and to justify refeeds, diet breaks, sleep and eating-schedule choices [3][4][5]. Studies have linked sleep restriction, fasting, exercise training and eating patterns to leptin levels [6][7][8][9].

Leptin is not a consumer product. Its synthetic analog metreleptin is a prescription drug for leptin deficiency and lipodystrophy [1][10]. Most people with obesity have high leptin but a blunted response to it, a state called leptin resistance, and researchers continue to debate how best to describe it [1][2]. Forum posters also disagree with each other about how much leptin explains dieting plateaus [3][11].
infobox: Mainly white and brown fat tissue; also placenta, muscle, stomach and others [1]
Higher from midnight to early morning; lower in late afternoon [1][13]

paras: Leptin affects how someone looks mainly by influencing how easy it is to eat less and stay lean. When energy stores fall during a diet, leptin falls too, and the brain responds with more hunger and lower energy output; in the opposite direction, rising fat mass raises leptin and is associated with appetite suppression [1][12]. That is why people in leanness-focused communities refer to leptin when planning deficits, refeed days and diet breaks [3][4][5].

Leptin also touches other things people care about: it is linked to puberty and fertility, bone metabolism and immune function, and lower levels are seen with higher testosterone and rise with estrogen and insulin [1].

The story begins in 1949 with obese mice at the Jackson Laboratory carrying the ob mutation, followed in the 1960s by Douglas Coleman's identification of a second obesity mutation, db, and his experiments pointing to a circulating factor [1]. In 1990 Rudolph Leibel and Jeffrey Friedman mapped the db gene region, and in 1994 Friedman's laboratory reported positional cloning of the mouse obese gene and its human counterpart in Nature [1][2]. The paper's authors suggested the gene product might be part of a signalling pathway from fat tissue regulating the size of fat stores [2]. Roger Guillemin suggested the name leptin [1].

In 1995 Jose Caro's laboratory found that obesity in humans was generally not due to ob mutations and that leptin resistance was likely, and the db gene was shown to encode the leptin receptor [1]. A first human leptin mutation was described in 1997, and eight have since been reported, all causing severe early-onset obesity [1]. Coleman and Friedman received major awards, including the Gairdner Award (2005) and the Shaw Prize (2009); Wikipedia notes that Leibel was not a co-author on the 1994 paper and received less recognition, a topic covered in Ellen Ruppel Shell's 2002 book The Hungry Gene [1].

The leptin receptor is encoded by LEPR, which produces six forms; only the long form, Ob-Rb, signals within cells, through the JAK-STAT and MAPK pathways [1]. In the lateral hypothalamus leptin suppresses hunger by counteracting neuropeptide Y and anandamide, and in the medial hypothalamus it promotes satiety by increasing alpha-MSH [1]. Without leptin or its receptor, uncontrolled hunger and obesity can result [1].

Most people with obesity have high leptin but respond to it poorly, which Wikipedia compares to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes. Proposed causes include impaired transport into the brain by high triglycerides and defects in the JAK-STAT and PI3K signalling pathways [1]. Reviews describe further proposed mechanisms such as SOCS3 upregulation and endoplasmic reticulum stress, many of them studied only in animals [12][13].

Some researchers suggest leptin works mainly as a starvation signal, so resistance could be an evolutionary advantage [1]. A 2020 Diabetes article by Zhao and colleagues argued that the concept needs rethinking, proposing that lowering bioactive leptin in obesity may improve sensitivity and that leptin therapy has not worked for diet-induced obesity [2]. A mouse study of a body-weight regulator independent of leptin was also discussed on Hacker News [14].

Metreleptin, a recombinant leptin analog, was approved in Japan in 2013, in the United States in February 2014 for complications of leptin deficiency in generalized lipodystrophy, in the EU in 2018 as Myalepta, and in Canada in January 2024 [1][10][13]. In a phase 3 open-label trial summarised on Grokipedia, HbA1c fell from 8.0 to 6.7 percent in 48 patients [13]. Reported side effects include hypoglycaemia, weight loss, injection-site reactions and headache, and the label carries a boxed warning for T-cell lymphoma, mainly in acquired generalised lipodystrophy [10][13]. In England the NHS began funding treatment for congenital leptin deficiency in April 2019 [1].

Investigational uses include nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, anorexia nervosa and hypothalamic amenorrhea [10][13]. A 2022 randomised trial found leptin increased hepatic triglyceride export through a vagal mechanism in humans [15]. For genetic obesity due to defects in the leptin-melanocortin pathway, a 2025 review describes the targeted drug setmelanotide, with naltrexone-bupropion and GLP-1 analogues showing similar benefits in small observational studies [2].

In a 2005 inpatient study of ten people (three never obese, seven obese) maintaining a 10 percent weight loss lowered energy expenditure, muscle work efficiency, sympathetic tone and thyroid hormones; giving twice-daily leptin that restored pre-weight-loss levels returned these measures to baseline. The authors proposed that the weight-reduced state resembles relative leptin insufficiency [2].

Researchers have since tested intermittent energy restriction against continuous restriction for effects on adaptive thermogenesis; one planned randomised trial in 74 women with obesity compares alternating restriction and balance weeks [2]. Reviews of weight loss plateaus and of dieters' cheat meals also cover hormonal and psychological responses [2].

A randomised crossover study at the University of Chicago in 12 healthy men found that partial sleep restriction was associated with lower leptin, higher ghrelin and increased hunger and appetite [6]. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 studies (2,250 participants) found higher ghrelin in short sleepers and higher leptin in experimental sleep-deprivation subgroups, differing from the 2004 trial's direction for leptin [7].

A 2020 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (425 participants) found that breakfast skipping reduced body weight by about half a kilogram compared with eating breakfast, without a significant difference in percent body fat [16]. A 2024 meta-analysis of 19 trials (568 participants) found time-restricted eating combined with exercise likely reduced body mass and fat mass compared with a control diet plus exercise [8]. A trial in men with type 2 diabetes and obesity compared aerobic and resistance training for effects on leptin and metabolic parameters [9].

sections.h: Leptin in dieting and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation and other fitness forums, leptin comes up as an explanation for slowed fat loss in long diets. One poster writes that people counting calories but not losing weight should consider leptin's hunger response and its effect on fat storage [4]. Another argues that very large carbohydrate refeeds were meant to bolster leptin and metabolism, a theory a writer in the same discussion says the science does not support [11]. Others describe 'resetting leptin' with a high-calorie day [5], or suggest that prolonged starvation produced a leptin deficiency after which regaining a little weight was not enough [17].

Poster JamesBrawn007 calls the idea that extended deficits lower leptin and slow metabolism a 'bro myth' while saying a planned refeed can still work as a psychological reward [3]. Users of GLP-1 drugs also speculate about leptin sensitivity when they describe a loss of food noise [18]. Wikipedia describes the Rosedale diet, built on Ron Rosedale's ideas about leptin, as lacking scientific support, citing a 2015 critique by Harriet Hall in Science-Based Medicine [19].

Human trials have measured leptin as an outcome of sleep, diet and exercise changes [6][7][8][9][16] and tested leptin replacement in weight-reduced people, lipodystrophy and fatty liver [15][2][10]. The 2005 low-dose leptin study in ten participants is among the studies cited when discussing metabolic adaptation to weight loss [2]. Reviews summarise leptin's role in obesity [12].

lore.intro: Leptin is a common talking point in cutting, refeed and plateau discussions on T Nation and similar fitness forums, where users disagree about how much it explains [3][4][5][11].

timeline.event: Obese mice at the Jackson Laboratory lead to discovery of the ob mutation.[1]
Douglas Coleman identifies a second obesity mutation, db, and a circulating factor.[1]
Rudolph Leibel and Jeffrey Friedman map the db gene region.[1]
Friedman laboratory reports positional cloning of the obese gene and its human homologue in Nature; Roger Guillemin suggests the name leptin.[1][2]
Caro's laboratory finds ob mutations are not common in human obesity, pointing to leptin resistance; the db gene is shown to encode the leptin receptor.[1]
Rosenbaum, Leibel and colleagues report that low-dose leptin reverses metabolic adaptations to reduced weight in ten subjects.[2]
Metreleptin approved in Europe as Myalepta.[1][13]
NHS England begins funding treatment for congenital leptin deficiency.[1]
